common_name: Canford Siberian Iris (Darker-Blue Self Sport of Bluecape)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Canford is a darker-blue Siberian iris raised by self-pollinating 'Bluecape'.

directions: Canford arose from self-pollinating 'Bluecape' and carries a deeper, more saturated blue self flower than its parent, with the fine violet veining of 'Bluecape' reduced to only a faint trace on the falls. Like other cultivars from this breeding line, it forms a tidy clump of narrow, grassy foliage on wiry stems well suited to a mixed border or pond margin. Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full sun to light shade, where it tolerates wetter conditions than bearded iris and can go several years between divisions. Lift and divide crowded clumps in early fall or right after spring bloom to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Cloudbank Ginny Leucadendron (Pastel Pink-Blushed Cut-Foliage Conebush)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in sharply drained, lean, phosphorus-poor, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Cloudbank Ginny is a softer-colored Leucadendron cultivar grown alongside 'Safari Sunset' and 'Wilson's Wonder' in the cut-foliage trade. Never use standard fertilizer, which is toxic to proteas at normal phosphorus levels.

directions: Cloudbank Ginny is grown alongside the deep-red 'Safari Sunset' and the compact 'Wilson's Wonder' in the international cut-foliage trade, prized for softer, pastel pink-and-cream bract color that gives florists an alternative to the more common crimson-toned Leucadendron selections. The plant forms an upright, bushy shrub with narrow, leathery gray-green leaves that recede behind the colorful bract clusters at the branch tips as temperatures cool. Like other Leucadendron selections, it demands sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; ordinary garden fertilizer at normal phosphate levels can quickly kill it, so use a protea-formulated low-phosphorus feed or none at all. Cut stems through the cool season for arrangements, and shape the plant lightly once the main color display fades to keep growth dense.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) PlantZAfrica
